title: What Does the Bible Say About Caring for Creation?
subtitle: The first job God ever gave a human being was to tend a garden, and we have spent most of history forgetting it. What Scripture says about the keeping of the earth, why creation care is neither nature worship nor a partisan slogan, and how the body and the soil bear witness to the same Maker.

parts.title: The Subject You Have Learned to Flinch From
parts.body:
Say the words out loud and watch yourself flinch. Creation care. The environment. The earth. You feel your shoulders rise, because the words have been taken, conscripted into a fight that has nothing to do with your faith and everything to do with which side you are supposed to be on. You have been trained to hear them as a tribal signal, and so before you can think a single thought about the actual world God made, a reflex fires that sorts the topic into a column, and the column comes with a whole set of assumptions about the kind of person who cares.

So you have done what most of us have done. You have let the subject go. If caring about the earth means joining a tribe whose other commitments you cannot share, you would rather not care, and you have quietly filed the whole matter under things faithful people do not need to think about, or worse, things faithful people are suspicious of. Meanwhile a quieter unease sits underneath, because you have read Genesis, and you have a vague memory that the first thing God gave a human being to do had something to do with a garden, and you cannot quite square your shrug with that memory.

Or maybe you flinch from the other direction. Maybe you have absorbed a reverence for nature that has slid, without your quite noticing, into something like worship, an instinct to treat the wild as sacred in itself, the planet as a kind of deity to be served, humanity as a stain upon it. And somewhere a different unease sits underneath that, because you sense that this too is not quite Christian, that to worship the creation rather than the Creator is the oldest mistake there is, and you do not know how to love the earth deeply without sliding into adoring it.

Here is the trouble underneath both flinches. You have only ever been handed two options, and both are counterfeits. One says the material world barely matters because it is all going to burn anyway, so use it up and look to heaven. The other says the material world is everything, the only sacred thing there is, and humanity its enemy. You stand between two idols, exploitation and worship, and you have not been shown the ancient third thing that is neither.

Let me name it plainly before we go on. The keeping of the earth is not a partisan cause you may take or leave depending on your tribe, and it is not a religion that divinizes the dirt. It is the first vocation God ever gave a human being, older than the fall, older than every political party by several thousand years, and it belongs to the church not because the church has gone green but because the church reads Genesis. The garden was given to be kept long before anyone made it a slogan, and the keeping is yours whether or not the slogan ever was.

parts.title: Why the Keeping Is Not Optional
parts.body:
The stakes here are not first about the planet's future, though that is real. They are about whether we will obey the first command God ever gave or quietly delete it because it has become politically inconvenient. God put the man in the garden to work it and keep it, and the church does not get to edit that line out of Scripture because the surrounding culture has made the topic awkward. When we let a partisan reflex decide which of God's commands we are allowed to take seriously, we have handed the tribe an authority over our consciences that belongs to the Word alone, and we have made ourselves captive to a politics rather than to Christ. That captivity, more than any policy, is what is at stake.

The second stake is the witness, because the watching world has noticed the deletion. The skeptic has heard Christians profess that the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof, that the heavens declare the glory of God, that every creature was made by Christ and for Christ, and then has watched many Christians treat the actual creation with a carelessness indistinguishable from contempt, as if the doctrine of a good Creator had no consequences for how his works are handled. The gap is a public sermon against the gospel. When believers use up the world as though it were disposable, the world concludes that we do not really believe God made it, and a powerful witness to the Creator is forfeited at exactly the moment the culture is most anxious about the earth.

The third stake is the poor, which is where this domain stops being abstract. The degradation of creation is never felt equally. The poisoned river, the eroded soil, the rising water, the foul air, these fall first and hardest on those without the means to move away from them, so that the way we keep or fail to keep the earth is inseparable from the way we love or fail to love the neighbor. To shrug at the keeping of creation is very often, in practice, to shrug at the suffering of the vulnerable who live downstream and downwind of our carelessness. The command to keep the garden and the command to love the neighbor turn out to be one command wearing two faces.

And the fourth stake is the integrity of our own faith, because a Christianity that despises the body and the earth has stopped being Christian. The faith confesses a God who made matter and called it good, who took on flesh and a digestive system, who was buried in the ground and rose in a body, and who promises not the escape of souls from a doomed planet but the renewal of all things, a new heaven and a new earth. To treat the material creation as worthless is to deny the incarnation and the resurrection at once, to confess a gnostic ghost rather than the Lord who made dirt and became dust. The keeping of the earth is not a peripheral add-on to the faith. It is a test of whether we actually believe what the faith confesses about the goodness of what God has made.

parts.title: Work It and Keep It
parts.body:
Begin in the garden, with the first job description God ever issued. The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it. Sit with both verbs. To work it, to cultivate, to draw out the latent fruitfulness of the ground, to make the wild place flourish under a tending hand. And to keep it, and the Hebrew word is shamar, the same word used for guarding, watching over, protecting, the word a shepherd uses for his flock and a watchman for his city. The first vocation of humanity is not to use the earth and not to leave it untouched but to keep it, to guard and tend the garden as something entrusted, not owned. This is the original human calling, given before sin entered the world, and nothing that came after cancelled it.

Notice that this keeping flows from a particular standing. God made human beings in his image and told them to have dominion over the earth, to fill it and subdue it, and the word dominion has been badly abused, read as a license to plunder. But dominion in Scripture is never tyranny. The king who images God rules as God rules, and God's rule over creation is generous, sustaining, attentive to the smallest sparrow, the very opposite of exploitation. To exercise dominion as God's image-bearer is to rule the way the true King rules, by serving the flourishing of what is under your care. The dominion mandate is not a permit to consume the garden. It is a commission to keep it the way a good king keeps a kingdom, for the good of everything in it.

And the earth is not finally ours to begin with. The land is mine, God says in Leviticus, and you are sojourners and tenants with me. The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell in it, the psalmist sings. We are not owners. We are tenants in a world that belongs to Another, accountable to the Landlord for how we have treated his property, and a tenant who trashes the house he was lent has insulted its owner. This single conviction, that the earth is God's and not ours, dismantles both idols at once. It refuses exploitation, because you do not get to wreck what is not yours. And it refuses worship, because you do not bow down to a house, however lovely, when you know its Maker.

Scripture builds the keeping right into the law. The land itself was to receive a Sabbath, lying fallow every seventh year so the soil could rest, and the same law that gave the land its rest gave its gleanings to the poor, binding creation care and neighbor love together in a single command. The fruit trees of a besieged city were not to be cut down, for is the tree of the field a man, that you should besiege it. The animals were to share in the Sabbath rest. The law of Israel treats the land, the creatures, and the poor as a single fabric of care, woven together under the one God who made them all, and tearing any thread tears the whole.

Then the New Testament lifts the whole creation into the work of Christ, and this is where the vision becomes vast. All things were created through him and for him, Paul writes of Christ, and in him all things hold together, not only souls, all things, the seas and the soil and the sparrows. And the creation, Paul says in Romans, was subjected to futility and groans like a woman in labor, waiting eagerly for the revealing of the children of God, because the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay. The earth is not a disposable stage that will be struck and discarded. It is a fellow sufferer of the fall and a fellow heir of the redemption, groaning toward the same renewal we are, and its future is not the incinerator but the resurrection.

For the end is not the escape of souls from a burning world. It is a new heaven and a new earth, the holy city coming down out of heaven to the earth, God dwelling with his people in a renewed creation. The Bible opens in a garden and closes in a garden city, with the tree of life and the river of life running through it, and the whole arc declares that God's purpose was never to rescue us out of his creation but to restore his creation and us together within it. We keep the garden now, however imperfectly, because we believe in the gardener God who will make all things new, and our tending is a small rehearsal of the renewal he has promised. The body and the soil are not luggage to be left behind. They are the very things God means to redeem.

parts.title: Stewards, Gnostics, and the Long Christian Care of the Earth
parts.body:
The earliest and fiercest battle the church fought over creation was against the Gnostics, and it set the course for everything after. The Gnostics taught that the material world was the botched work of a lesser, malevolent deity, a prison of matter from which the spark of the soul must escape, and they despised the body, the earth, and the God who made them. The church answered with a thunderous no. Irenaeus of Lyons, in the second century, insisted that one God made all things, that the flesh is capable of salvation, that the same God who formed Adam from the dust will raise that dust in glory. The creed confesses God the Father, maker of heaven and earth, and means it. The church's earliest defining fight was a defense of the goodness of the material creation against those who called it worthless, and every Christian who treats the earth as disposable has quietly rejoined the heresy the church died to refute.

The monastic tradition turned this conviction into a way of life on the land. The Benedictines and especially the Cistercians settled in wild and ruined places and tended them into fruitfulness, draining marshes, restoring soil, planting forests, treating agricultural labor not as a curse but as a holy participation in the keeping of the garden. Their work was governed by stability and care, by the conviction that you do not strip a place and move on but settle into it and tend it across generations. The monasteries became, for centuries, schools of careful husbandry, demonstrating that the keeping of the earth and the love of God were not two things but one, prayer and labor woven into a single rhythm on a particular patch of ground.

The figure the whole tradition remembers most vividly is Francis of Assisi, who in the thirteenth century looked at the sun and the moon, the wind and the water, the birds and even death itself, and called them brother and sister, members with him of one created family under one Father. Francis was no nature-worshipper. His Canticle of the Creatures praises not the creation but the Creator through the creation, the most High and the good Lord to whom belong all praise and glory, and the creatures are his fellow worshippers, not his gods. He held the exact balance the modern world has lost, a love for every creature so tender it could call a wolf brother, grounded entirely in the worship of the God who made them, never sliding into the divinization of the dirt.

The deeper theological grammar runs through the whole tradition in the idea of the two books, that God reveals himself in two volumes, the book of Scripture and the book of nature, and that to read the creation rightly is to read it as the work of its Author. The heavens declare the glory of God, and the medieval and Reformation theologians alike treated the natural world as a theater of God's glory, a creation shot through with the signature of its Maker. John Calvin called the world a dazzling theater of divine glory and a beautiful book in which even the unlettered could read of God. To care for the creation, in this grammar, is to handle reverently a book that speaks of God on every page, and to despoil it is to deface a revelation.

The modern severing came later, and the church was complicit in it. As an industrial age learned to see nature as mere raw material, inert stuff to be extracted and used, a thin and selective Christianity sometimes lent its voice, seizing on the language of dominion to baptize exploitation and on the promise of heaven to dismiss the earth as a doomed and disposable stage. At the same time the recoil against that exploitation often swung to the opposite idol, a romantic and finally pagan reverence that worshipped nature and cast humanity as its disease. Both severed what the tradition held together. The recovery in our own time, across the breadth of the church, has been a return to the older and deeper word that was there all along, that the earth is the Lord's, that we are its tenants and not its owners, that the keeping of the garden is the first human vocation, and that this conviction belongs not to a political tribe but to the faith once delivered to the saints.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: A believer can learn a great deal from those who study the earth and humanity's place upon it, the scientists, the farmers, the writers who have attended closely to soil, climate, and the web of living things. All truth is God's truth. What follows takes five bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly, and tests each against Scripture, because every account of nature and our place in it carries a hidden picture of what the earth is and what a human being is for, and that picture is where the keeping is finally won or lost.

secular.source: The Sand County Almanac and the land ethic
secular.author: Aldo Leopold
secular.whatItGetsRight: Leopold articulated a land ethic that enlarged the boundaries of moral community to include the soil, waters, plants, and animals, arguing that a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the living community. He saw, with the eye of a working ecologist, that everything is connected, that careless use of one part wounds the whole, and that human beings are members of the land community, not merely its conquerors. This is a recovery of the keeping that the dominion-as-plunder reading had lost.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Leopold rightly restores humanity to membership in the created community and stops short of the standing Scripture gives that membership. His land ethic grounds our obligation in ecological interdependence alone, which can tell you that harming the land harms you but cannot finally tell you why the land matters when it does not. Scripture grounds the keeping deeper, in the land belonging to God and the human being bearing his image as a steward accountable to him, so that the earth is to be kept not merely because we depend on it but because it is the Lord's and we will answer to him for it. Membership becomes stewardship, and the obligation gains a Person to whom it is owed.

secular.source: Silent Spring and the founding of modern ecology
secular.author: Rachel Carson
secular.whatItGetsRight: Carson exposed, with rigorous evidence, how human intervention ripples through the web of life in ways we neither intend nor foresee, how a poison meant for one pest silences the songbirds of a whole spring. She awakened a generation to the truth that the creation is an intricate, interdependent order that careless power can unravel, and that our actions on the land carry consequences far beyond what we can see. This is a faithful reading of a creation more interconnected and more easily wounded than the exploiters assumed.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Carson saw the wound and the interconnection with prophetic clarity and worked within a frame that could name the damage but not the deeper disorder beneath it. Scripture agrees that creation is intricately ordered and grievously woundable, and locates the root of the damage where Carson's science cannot reach, in a human heart bent away from its Maker, exercising a dominion divorced from the God it was meant to image. The silenced spring is not only an ecological failure. It is a parable of a creature ruling without reference to the Creator, and the cure is not only better regulation but a reordered heart that keeps the garden as God's tenant rather than its tyrant.

secular.source: The Unsettling of America and agrarian thought
secular.author: Wendell Berry
secular.whatItGetsRight: Berry, a farmer and a Christian, has argued for half a century that the health of the soil, the community, and the human soul are one health, that a culture which treats land as a commodity to be used up and abandoned will use up its people the same way, and that the keeping of a particular place across generations is a moral and spiritual discipline. His vision of stewardship, rootedness, and limits is among the most profound recoveries of the keeping vocation in modern letters, and it is consciously biblical at its core.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Berry stands very close to the biblical vision, and where Scripture presses further is in the resurrection hope that his agrarian realism holds more loosely. Berry's care for the land can carry a melancholy sense of fighting a long, losing rear-guard against decline, keeping faith with a place that will likely be ruined anyway. Scripture keeps the same place with the same fidelity and does so in hope, because the creation that groans is promised liberation, the earth is not finally going down but being made new. The keeping is not a noble holding action against inevitable loss. It is a rehearsal of a renewal God has guaranteed, and that hope changes the keeping from grief into anticipation.

secular.author: Arne Naess and the deep ecology movement
secular.whatItGetsRight: Deep ecology rightly protests the arrogance of treating nature as mere resource for human use, insisting that the living world has worth in itself and not only as raw material for human projects, and that human beings have vastly overstepped, consuming and destroying with a self-regard that has wounded the whole community of life. Its critique of human hubris and its insistence on the intrinsic value of the non-human world echo a truth the exploiters denied, that the creatures matter to their Maker apart from their usefulness to us.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Deep ecology corrects the arrogance of exploitation and then overcorrects into the opposite idol, demoting the human being to one species among others with no special standing, and sometimes casting humanity as a kind of disease upon an otherwise pristine earth. Scripture holds the balance both extremes lose. The creatures do have worth before God apart from our use of them, the sparrow is not forgotten, and yet the human being uniquely bears God's image and is given the keeping of the rest, neither the lord who plunders nor the cancer to be removed but the steward who guards. To divinize nature and despise humanity is to flee one idol straight into another. The garden needs a keeper, not a worshipper and not an absence.

secular.author: The scientific consensus on environmental limits
secular.whatItGetsRight: The painstaking work of climate and earth-systems science has established, with the ordinary rigor of careful observation, that human activity is altering the conditions of the planet in ways that fall hardest on the poor and the unborn, and that the creation has limits which careless power can breach. This is honest reading of the book of nature, the kind of attentive observation of God's world that the wisdom tradition always honored, and the believer has no more reason to fear it than to fear a faithful weather report.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The science describes the limits and the damage and cannot, by itself, supply either the hope or the motive to act rightly within them. Left alone, the data tends toward two unbiblical poles, a paralyzing despair that the world is doomed, or a frantic technological pride that we will save ourselves. Scripture refuses both. It takes the limits seriously, for the earth is the Lord's and not infinite, and it neither despairs, because God will renew his creation, nor presumes, because we are tenants and not saviors. The believer reads the science gratefully, grieves the damage honestly, keeps the garden faithfully, and rests the final outcome in the hands of the One who has promised to make all things new.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who agree that the earth is the Lord's and that keeping it is a real vocation still differ on how that keeping should be pursued, whether chiefly through personal and local faithfulness or also through systemic and structural action. The disagreement is not over whether to care. Both sides care, and both refuse the partisan capture of the question. It is over where the keeping mainly happens. Hear each view at its strongest, because both are guarding something Scripture genuinely teaches.

views.view: Keeping begins with personal and local faithfulness
views.body: This view holds that the keeping of the garden is, first and most truly, a matter of how a particular person tends a particular place, and that the believer's primary calling is faithful stewardship in the concrete sphere God has actually given them. Advocates point to the agrarian wisdom of Scripture, the man set in his garden, the law of the fallow field, the tending of a place across generations, and they argue that grand systemic crusades easily become abstractions that change nothing while feeding pride, whereas the humble, daily disciplines of using less, wasting nothing, growing something, caring for the land and creatures in reach actually form a person into a keeper. They are wary of how quickly creation care at the structural level gets swallowed into partisan politics and ideological tribes, and they believe the surest way to keep the witness free of capture is to keep it local, embodied, and personal. So the wise course is to tend your own patch faithfully, to cultivate gratitude and restraint and care in the place you live, trusting that a people of genuine keepers will do more good than a movement of distant advocates. The danger this view guards against is real, a creation care that is all slogans and no soil, that signals concern at the level of policy while living as wastefully as everyone else, that has plenty of opinions about the planet and tends nothing it can touch. Against that, this view holds that the keeping God commanded was always hands in the dirt before it was anything else.

views.view: Keeping must also confront the systems that wound creation
views.body: This view holds that personal faithfulness, while essential, is not sufficient, because the gravest wounds to creation are inflicted by structures and systems no individual can heal alone, and that to confine the keeping to one's own backyard while the poison flows downstream to the poor is to mistake a private virtue for the whole command. Advocates point to the prophets, who confronted not only individual sins but the corrupt systems that ground the faces of the poor, and to the law of Israel itself, which built creation care into the structure of the society through the Sabbath of the land and the gleaning of the fields. They argue that since the degradation of creation falls hardest on the vulnerable, loving the neighbor requires addressing the systems that poison the neighbor's air and water, and that to refuse structural action in the name of staying out of politics is itself a political choice that protects the powerful. So the wise course is to tend your own place faithfully and also to lend your voice and effort to the larger keeping, working for just and wise stewardship at the scale where the real damage is done, while refusing to let any party own the cause. The danger this view guards against is also real, a privatized faith that polishes its own small virtue while the creation groans under harms its tidy habits never touch, that uses local faithfulness as an alibi for ignoring the suffering of those downwind. Against that, this view holds that the God who built the keeping into the very structure of Israel's common life means for his people to care about the structures, and that to love both the garden and the neighbor is to confront what wounds them both.

parts.title: What the Keeping Forms in a Person
parts.body:
The keeping of the earth is not only a thing we do to the world. It is a thing God does to us through the doing, slowly forming in the keeper a particular kind of person, one the culture of exploitation and the religion of nature-worship both fail to produce. To tend the garden as God's tenant is to be apprenticed, over years, into a way of being human that neither idol can teach.

It forms gratitude, the deep kind, the kind that receives the world as gift rather than seizing it as right. The exploiter takes, assuming the earth is his to use up. The nature-worshipper trembles before a creation with no giver behind it. But the keeper learns to receive each thing, the bread, the rain, the soil, the breath, as a gift from the hand of a Father, and gratitude reorders a person at the root, replacing the grasping that drives consumption with a receiving that knows itself dependent. The keeper of the garden becomes, almost without noticing, a person who says thank you, and a grateful person handles the world differently than a greedy one.

It forms humility, because to keep the earth as a tenant is to be daily reminded that you are not the owner. The work of tending soil and creatures will not let a person sustain the illusion of mastery for long, for the gardener learns quickly that he does not make things grow, he only tends what Another grows, that he is a creature among creatures, formed from the same dust he works, dependent on rain he cannot summon and seasons he cannot command. This humility is the opposite of both idols, refusing the exploiter's arrogance that the earth is his to dominate and the worshipper's despair that the human is a stain, settling instead into the right and lowly dignity of a steward who answers to a Lord.

It forms a love that runs from the creation to the Creator without stopping to worship the creature. The keeper learns to do what Francis did, to look at the sun and the soil and the sparrow and to be moved through them to the One who made them, so that attention to the world becomes a form of worship of its Author. This is the great balance the modern world has lost, the ability to love a thing deeply precisely because you love its Maker more, to be so secure in the Creator that you can adore the creation without divinizing it. The keeper grows into a person for whom the whole world has become, again, the dazzling theater of God's glory it always was, a book speaking of God on every page.

And it forms hope, the resurrection kind, which is the strangest and most durable thing the keeping produces. The keeper of the earth, who knows both the goodness of what God made and the futility to which it has been subjected, tends the garden in the confidence that the creation that groans is promised liberation, that the same God who will raise their body will renew the earth, that the keeping is not a holding action against inevitable loss but a rehearsal of a renewal already guaranteed. This hope frees the keeper from both the despair that says the world is doomed so why bother and the pride that says we must save the world ourselves. They keep the garden faithfully, neither saving it nor abandoning it, because they belong to the Gardener who has promised to make all things new, and their tending of the soil today is a small and stubborn act of faith in the new heaven and new earth he has pledged to bring. The body and the soil they care for now are the very things God means to redeem, and the keeper, knowing this, keeps them as one who has already glimpsed the garden city coming down.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: None of this is changed by being agreed with. The keeping of the earth is learned the way any vocation is learned, in small repeated acts over time, hands in the actual dirt, under the lordship of the God who owns it. None of what follows will heal the creation by Friday or settle every contested question about how. All of it will start to wear a groove if you stay with it, and the groove, the slow forming of a keeper out of a consumer, is the point. Begin where you are, in the place God has actually given you, with one thing, this week.

steps: Read Genesis 2 and Psalm 24 slowly, and let the two convictions land before any partisan reflex can fire. God put the man in the garden to work it and keep it. The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof. Receive the keeping as a command older than every party.

Examine your own flinch. Notice whether you have let a tribe decide for you that creation care is suspect, or whether you have slid toward revering nature as sacred in itself, and name the idol you are nearer to so the Word can correct it.

Practice one act of gratitude for the created world this week, eating a meal slowly with thanks to the Giver, walking outside and attending to one creature until it points you to its Maker, receiving the world as gift rather than taking it as right.

Reduce one habit of waste in your own household, the food thrown out, the thing bought and discarded, the resource used carelessly, not as a political statement but as a tenant's respect for property that belongs to God.

Read the creation care passages woven through the law, the Sabbath of the land, the gleaning for the poor, the sparing of the trees, and notice how God binds the keeping of the earth to the love of the neighbor. Let the connection reframe the subject as discipleship, not politics.

Tend something living with your own hands, a garden bed, a few plants, a patch of soil, a tree, and let the work teach your body what no argument can, that you do not make things grow, you only keep what Another grows.

Trace one line from your own use of the world to the neighbor who lives downstream of it, and let the love of neighbor enlarge your sense of the keeping beyond your own comfort to the vulnerable who bear the cost of carelessness.

Talk with believers across the usual tribal lines about creation care as a matter of Scripture rather than party, and practice holding the conviction free of the slogans, refusing to let either idol or either tribe own a command God gave the whole church.

Build a few keeping disciplines into the rhythm of your household, using less and wasting less as ordinary habits rather than occasional gestures, so that restraint and care become the normal texture of your life rather than a campaign.

Learn the place God has actually given you, its watershed, its soil, its creatures, its seasons, and grow into a keeper of that particular patch across time, because the keeping Scripture commands was always rooted in a place before it was anything else.

Discern your own calling in the larger keeping with wisdom, whether to lend your voice and effort to the structural care that confronts the systems wounding creation and the poor, and do it without surrendering to any party's capture of the cause.

Let the creation drive you to worship on purpose, returning often to the world as the theater of God's glory, reading the book of nature as a revelation of its Author, and letting attention to the soil and the sky deepen your adoration of the One who made them.

Grow into a settled keeper of the earth, neither exploiter nor worshipper, a tenant who tends God's property with gratitude, humility, and care across the long arc of a life, handing the keeping on to those who come after as it was handed to you.

Bind your care for creation and your care for the poor into a single love, so that the keeping of the garden and the loving of the neighbor are no longer two concerns but one obedience, woven together as the law of God wove them.

Refuse, year after year, the partisan capture of the question, holding the keeping of the earth as a matter of the ancient creedal faith, maker of heaven and earth, and modeling for a divided church a conviction that no tribe owns and the Word commands.

Keep the garden in hope, tending the soil and the body and the world in the confidence that the creation which groans is promised liberation, that your keeping now is a rehearsal of the renewal to come, until the day the garden city comes down and the Gardener makes all things, the body and the soil among them, new.

kicker: Creation and Our Keeping: Tending the Garden
